items.title: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day
items.excerpt: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day # Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day Jared Blikre Sun, October 18, 2026 at 6:33 AM CDT 3 min read Inflation is reaching fewer corners of the economy. That doesn't mean life is getting cheaper. Only about 38% of the roughly 175 categories in the Consumer Price Index rose faster than a 3% annual pace over the past six months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. That's down from 56% in May and the fewest since spring 2025. The count borrows a test from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who laid it out at Jackson Hole in August. He counts how many categories in the Fed's preferred PCE price gauge are rising faster than 3%, a gauge of how widespread inflation is. The Fed's goal is still 2%. BLS, Yahoo Finance "Too many categories are still posting increases above 3% on both a six- and 12-month basis," Warsh said after the Fed raised rates in September. By that yardstick, September looked better than its hotter-than-expected headline. The 12-month count slipped to about 47% from 51% in August. At the 2022 peak, about 4 in 5 categories topped 3%. In the two decades before the pandemic, about 1 in 3 typically did. A narrower spread strengthens the case for waiting, and traders have leaned that way. The bond market put the odds of a hike at the Oct. 27-28 meeting at about 17% by Friday's close, according to Bloomberg data — down from roughly 33% after Wednesday's CPI report. Warsh declined to preview his next move in remarks Friday before the International Monetary Fund. Some Fed officials want more evidence before moving. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called September's inflation report discouraging but told Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger he favors waiting before acting again. "We need to get more data," he said. ## The holdout categories are the expensive ones Electricity, rent, hospital services, and car repairs have all been rising faster than 3% over the past six months, after adjusting for seasonal swings. Gasoline is up about 34% from a year ago. Together, the categories still above the line make up at least 60% of the CPI basket, which the BLS weights by how much households spend on each item. Groceries show the other side of the problem. Grocery prices rose less than 2% over the past year, yet they're still up nearly a third since December 2019. Electricity is up 43% over the same stretch. BLS, Yahoo Finance Slower inflation means prices rise more slowly. It doesn't bring them back down, and the Fed has no intention of returning to 2019 prices. Not everyone sees progress. "There is little evidence of a cooling or a broad-based disinflationary impulse," RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas wrote Wednesday, pointing to trade, energy, and AI as sources of stubborn price pressure. He expects another quarter-point hike in December. The bond market leans his way on the longer view. Traders still price in about one full quarter-point increase by the Dec. 9 meeting and nearly three by September 2027. The next test arrives Oct. 29, when September PCE inflation is released, one day after the Fed decides. Next month's CPI report follows. If the six-month count holds below 40%, the case for waiting gets stronger. A return to 50% or more — near where it sat for most of the first half of the year — would put a hike back on the table. Watch rent and electricity. Until they cool, a shrinking count won't feel like relief. *Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.* *Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at **jaredblikre@yahooinc.com**.*

items.title: Bessent: ‘We Will Own the Economy,’ but 3.7% Inflation Is an Energy Shock
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON — Asked on Sunday when the administration would take responsibility for the economy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said “we will own the economy,” then called the price surge “an energy supply side shock” and said the country would “get to the other side of the Iran conflict.” The exchange on NBC’s “Meet the Press” began with moderator Kristen Welker citing the September figure: consumer prices up 3.7% from a year earlier, the fastest pace in five months. She asked whether the president’s policies were driving inflation. “Kristen, we have an energy shock,” Bessent answered. The same interview produced his remarks on Ukraine missile intelligence, which TEH reported separately. The numbers land 16 days before the midterms, as Welker noted at the top of the show, and NBC News called the September report the final CPI release before the vote. ... Welker then asked whether gas prices would come down by the new year. “Well, again, it will depend on what happens with the Iran conflict,” Bessent said. Earlier, according to NBC’s transcript, he had said energy markets would be “better supplied than they were” on the other side of that conflict. The transcript contains no date for relief, and no figure for how far prices would fall.

That's prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach., The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics estimates the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 related to energy. Motorists and airline passengers so far have borne the clearest consequences from disrupted Middle East oil shipments. items.excerpt: Trump’s approval rating slips again, and a deadly incident at a youth soccer game: Weekend Rundown # Trump’s approval rating slips again, and a deadly incident at a youth soccer game: Weekend Rundown Plus, the pope is discharged from the hospital, and erosion is changing California’s coastline. Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. NBC News Oct. 18, 2026, 6:00 PM EDT By Amina Kilpatrick, Mark Hodge and Kayla Hayempour Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in President Donald Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterms, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey. Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. A majority of Americans view the president’s administration as uniquely corrupt, even as they look skeptically at corruption in both parties. And they say Trump is failing to improve their material financial conditions. The president’s approval rating slipped to 34% among U.S. adults, a second-term low in this poll, while his disapproval rating rose to 66%. Americans continue to hold a negative view of Democrats, too. Among adults, just 43% view the Democratic Party favorably. ## Boy and man killed, 10 injured after woman drives through youth soccer game in Kansas A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed and 10 other people were injured when a woman drove a truck through a youth soccer game at a city sports complex in Wichita, Kansas, Saturday afternoon, police said. The 34-year-old driver was in custody, though it wasn’t immediately clear whether the incident at the Stryker Sports Complex was intentional, police said. “She has been cooperative up to this point in the investigation,” Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said at an evening news conference. There were two children in the truck, Moses said. One of the woman’s children had a game at the complex, though at a different field. The injured include five children, ages 5 to 9, as well as five men and women 28 to 68 years old, he said. ## ‘Meet the Press’: Zelenskyy warns U.S. against ‘historic mistake’ 25:00 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S. formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake,” but said he still sees Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill. “We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.” Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress. The move came days after U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” Zelenskyy said, leaving Ukraine blind to incoming ballistic missiles. Limits have also been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercepting jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe SpaceX imposed the Starlink limits in response to a “message from American government.” Amid escalating tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dodged three times when asked whether Ukraine is an ally of the United States. “We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” Bessent told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the second time he was asked whether the U.S. considers Ukraine an ally. (Earlier, Bessent said U.S. support includes providing intelligence, Starlink support and allowing NATO to purchase U.S. weapons to resell to Ukraine.) Asked for a third time, the treasury secretary simply said, “I’m not the secretary of state. I’m not the president.” ## Notable quote > It seems to me that this won’t stop Putin. On the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that there is such support. > > Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Zelenskyy responded to Trump suspending new sanctions against Russia that Congress had passed. Trump had signed the legislation, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. ## Politics in brief - ‘ No Kings’: Rallies opposing Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections. - D.C. makeover: Trump announced plans to redevelop the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C., which has been at the center of a legal battle over his renovation push. - Foreign endorsement: Trump endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the longtime Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week’s parliamentary election. ## Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery Pope Leo XIV leaves Gemelli University Hospital in Rome on Saturday. Tiziana Fabi / AFP via Getty Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital Saturday after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with his surgeon saying he could make a full recovery within about 10 days. Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News there were “no clinical reasons” why the pontiff should not make his planned trip to Latin America next month. Leo, who had been recovering at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday, walked out unaided and spent a couple of minutes speaking to well-wishers. He appeared to accept a gift of a homemade smiling figure of the pope before getting into a car to return to the Vatican. He thanked well-wishers on Sunday as he recited the Angelus prayer from the window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace. ## ‘The house was toast’: Surf swallows California homes Several houses along the 6400 block of Seaside Walk at the Peninsula in Long Beach, Calif., on Thursday. Adam Amengual for NBC News The worst of El Niño is still months away, but Southern California’s fragile coastline is already being transformed by record-setting king tides and storm surges. An unusually active hurricane season triggered a trio of storms that pummeled Hawaii and Mexico earlier this year. The historic weather pattern claimed more than a dozen homes along the shore in Long Beach, swallowing up boardwalks and portions of the Pacific Coast Highway farther south. “This is just a little bit of a taste of what we will see in the future,” warned Timu Gallien with the Coastal Flood Lab at the University of California, Los Angeles. ## Golden State Valkyries take Game 1 of WNBA Finals over Atlanta Dream Game 1 of the 2026 WNBA Finals. Getty Images In front of a sold-out sea of purple at the Chase Center, the Golden State Valkyries shook off an early deficit and shooting struggles to beat the Atlanta Dream 68-64 and take Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. Valkyries star Gabby Williams led all scorers with 26 points on 8-of-22 shooting. She hit two free throws with 4.1 seconds remaining to ice the game. Allisha Gray led the Dream with 19 points on 5-of-19 shooting but was held scoreless in the fourth quarter. The Valkyries forced 12 Atlanta turnovers and scored 17 points off them. Golden State center Kiah Stokes recorded four blocks in the first half to add to the team’s total of 10. ## In case you missed it - Police arrested at least 1,800 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during demonstrations over rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. - Canada’s defense minister said four people were killed and multiple others were injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire. - A man died after being shot during a dispute at a subway station in Manhattan’s Theater District, according to police. - Val Chmerkovskiy received a one-week suspension on “Dancing with the Stars” after a comment he made on social media. - A 71-year-old man died after an alligator attacked him while he was fishing, authorities said. Scott Bessent, Steve Kornacki, Lanhee Chen, Hallie Jackson and Steve Ricchetti Oct. 18, 2026, 12:22 PM EDT KRISTEN WELKER: This Sunday, hard sell. With just 16 days until the midterms, President Trump barnstorms the country in a final push for Republicans as inflation rises and control of Congress hangs in the balance. PRES. DONALD TRUMP: That war is going to end very soon, and when it does, your prices are going to come tumbling down. They already are. REP. ASHLEY HINSON: We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it. JOSH TUREK: I know that you’re struggling just to keep food on the table, a roof above your head and keep gas in your tank. KRISTEN WELKER: I’ll talk to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock and Republican Senator James Lankford. Plus, Steve Kornacki with our new Decision Desk poll. And, betrayed. President Trump suspends sweeping new sanctions against Russia just weeks after signing them into law as Putin continues his deadly attacks on Ukraine. PRES. VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: We hope that President, his team, will be on our side. KRISTEN WELKER: I’ll talk exclusively to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy who says he feels betrayed by President Trump. Plus, Musk money. Elon Musk pours millions into the fight for Texas. Can his money help Republicans hold the seat? Joining me for insight and analysis are NBC News Senior Washington correspondent Hallie Jackson, former Biden White House senior adviser Steve Ricchetti and Lanhee Chen, a fellow at the Hoover Institution. Welcome to Sunday, it’s Meet the Press. ... News in Washington, the longest-running show in television history, this is Meet the Press with Kristen Welker. KRISTEN WELKER: Good Sunday morning. With just 16 days until the midterms, the political map is now shifting. The Cook Political Report has moved 11 more House races toward Democrats as Republicans face growing voter frustration over the economy. NBC News chief data analyst Steve Kornacki is here with me at the big board with the results of our brand new NBC News Decision Desk poll. Steve, quite a snapshot, 16 days out. STEVE KORNACKI: Yeah, Kristen. What you’re seeing is the climate that’s propelling the shift you’re talking about there. So first of all, the big-picture question here: Trump’s approval rating. Our Decision Desk poll, again this is registered voters here, bit of a wider net than you see in the other polls out there right now. But 39% here, the approval rating. And again, this continues to be the story, asking, “Do you approve of Trump on inflation here?” Only 31%, 34% on Iran. He does do better when it comes to immigration. But voters saying that it’s more inflation, it’s the economy, it’s cost of living. That’s more front and center to them than immigration, than some of the other issues. And he’s got very low numbers right there. Also seeing this: the generic ballot here, “Which party would you like to see control Congress?” The advantage in this Decision Desk poll here for Democrats is nine points there. You know, if you went back to Trump’s first midterm in 2018, bad one for Republicans, it was a tick under that. So nine right now there. Getting toward the high side for Democrats, very alarming for Republicans. And again, what’s driving this? We’re asking folks, your financial situation, compare it to a year ago, how is it? 44% saying, “worse now than a year ago.” By the way, among Independents, outright majority, 53% say worse now than a year ago. Again, it gets to that climate here, gas prices, two-thirds here in this poll saying, “This is a serious problem,” the cost of gas, the cost of fuel for them and for their family. This is interesting too I thought Kristen though. Within what we think of as the president’s base, among Republicans in this poll, look at the difference here. Among those who call themselves MAGA Republicans, his approval rating is still 93%, it’s not bad. Among those who say, “No, I’m more of a traditional Republican,” 63%. And compare this to a year ago, look at this, the MAGA number is not moving that much. This number is. And the other thing picking up here in the poll, “How do you identify yourself,” we’re asking Republicans. “Do you call yourself a MAGA Republican or a traditional Republican?” Look at how the balance has shifted. It’s now 56% who say traditional Republican. Look at where the number was in 2025. The majority was on the MAGA side. So that shifted too. We do say though, end on a note of caution here, a note of uncertainty. We showed you that generic ballot here, but break it down this way, asking folks, “Will you definitely vote in the midterm?” There’s a motivation edge here for Democrats. They lead by 12 on the generic ballot with “definitely.” That’s about 80% of the folks in the poll. But those who say “probably” or “no,” and believe it or not, some folks who say “no” to a poll do end up voting, the Republicans have the advantage with those who are not sure they’re going to be voting right now. So the more Republicans succeed in expanding the electorate there, they might be able to bring that generic ballot down some. ... SEN. RAPHAEL WARNOCK: Let’s be clear. Democrats can absolutely win in these states. In fact, the road to a Democratic majority in both houses of Congress is in the South. I spent the last week moving through North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Mississippi. When you look at these states, when you look at a state like Texas, the South will have an outsized role in determining who has the majority. And I worry, to be very honest, that Democrats are missing a real opportunity to invest in a serious and sustained way in the South. If we would just lean in and stay in, through the election, and after the election, the kind of victory you saw us achieve here in Georgia, it is achievable in a place like Mississippi and all across the South. ... I know you’re headed to Michigan next week, there’s a big Senate race there between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers. El-Sayed’s primary challenger, Haley Stevens, who of course lost to El-Sayed, did carry Michael counties with large Black populations. She said this. She said that Rogers, quote, is “working the Black community harder and more successfully than we have ever seen a Republican do or at least that I can remember ever.” Senator, what do you think El-Sayed needs to do in order to win over Black voters? ... Listen, Black voters are suffering like all of our voters, like the American people in general. It is in our best interest to make sure that Abdul El-Sayed wins this election. We are witnessing a president, Donald Trump, along with his henchmen and the extreme court gerrymander Black voters, especially in the South. Michigan voters have a role to play in that because they are trying to diminish our voices. And so I’ll be in Michigan this week campaigning. We’ve got to turn out our whole coalition. ... To be very clear, I am sharply focused on the midterm elections. This is a deeply consequential election. We’ve got to put some guard rails on this president. And Jon Ossoff and I are aligned on this issue. There’s nothing more important than defeating his pathetic opponent, Mike Collins. We’ve got to win victories in the House and the Senate and I remember sharply focused on that. ... So the president has the ability under the statute to be able to look at national interests. And he came back and he said, “Our gas prices are very high right now.” The sanctions are specifically targeted on energy. He’s trying to walk this fine balance between trying to be able to put pressure on Russia but also to be able to help the American people. So he is choosing the American people first, is what he’s doing. And if anyone’s shocked that this president’s focused on American voters first, they should have listened to him the last several years. He is very focused on that. But at the same time, the president is sharing intelligence information with the Ukrainians. He is providing weapon systems to the Ukrainians. He’s put other sanctions on Russian oil companies. So the pressure is on Russia from this president. So any belief that President Trump is aligning with President Putin is not true. He’s trying to get both of them to the table. But he is definitely providing continual support to the Ukrainians. ... It’s great to have you back. Let’s start on inflation, these new inflation numbers we got this week. Consumer prices rose in September at the fastest pace in five months, to 3.7%. Are the president’s policies driving up inflation? SECRETARY SCOTT BESSENT: Kristen, we have an energy shock. And if you look underneath the hood in the numbers, core inflation has been very flat before this month, and it’d been down for four months in a row. So core inflation is down. The food is below the Fed’s targets. The prescription drugs have had the biggest decrease in history. Rents are down. So this is an energy shock. We will get to the other side of the Iran conflict, and those prices will come down. ... we come back, with just 16 days to go, the battle for Congress is shifting toward Democrats. The panel is next.l KRISTEN WELKER: Elon Musk is pouring millions into the fight for Texas. Will it help Republicans? You’re also dealing with the quality of the ... Ken Paxton has his own headwinds. And it comes as this week, Elon Musk donated a staggering $158 million to PACs supporting Ken Paxton. items.excerpt: # 16 days until midterms, Trump rallies GOP as Johnson predicts Republicans will hold House President Donald Trump is intensifying his campaign push for Republican candidates as Democrats target the president and House Speaker Mike Johnson works to defend the GOP’s narrow majority. ## WHAT TO KNOW - President Donald Trump rallied Republicans in Kentucky over the weekend, tying the party’s midterm prospects to his second-term agenda and warning that Democrats could reverse his policies. - House Speaker Mike Johnson says Republicans will retain control of the chamber despite voter frustration over high prices, the war with Iran and the GOP’s narrow margin. - Democrats are intensifying attacks on Trump while focusing on competitive Senate races in Georgia, Michigan and Texas and working to regain control of Congress. ... ## Former Biden pollster warns Democrats falling short on youth turnout Kellyanne Conway warned Sunday that Democratic enthusiasm in polls may not translate into votes, while former Biden campaign pollster Celinda Lake said her party has fallen short on investing in youth turnout. “Participation in a poll is not the same as participation at the polls,” Conway said on “Fox News Sunday.” The Fox News contributor argued some Republicans are reluctant to answer surveys and said competitive Senate races remain “on a razor’s edge.” Lake countered that Democrats lead on enthusiasm but urged voters against letting favorable polling keep them home. “It’s important for people at this point in time not to listen to the polls,” she said. “And when a pollster tells you that, you know you should believe it.” ... off Bill Clinton’s potential impact on Florida’s elections Sunday, arguing the Democratic Party has moved beyond the former president. ... ## Newsom warns 2028 may lack ‘free and fair election’ unless Democrats win midterms California Gov. Gavin Newsom warned Democrats that a “free and fair election” in 2028 could hinge on their winning key congressional races this year. “It is all on the line in 2026,” Newsom said in a video shared on X. “Do not focus on 2028.” “We may not have a free and fair election in 2028 unless Maggie is back in the majority and Chris is in the United States Senate,” he added, referring to New Hampshire Democratic Reps. Maggie Goodlander and Chris Pappas. Newsom offered no evidence in the clip to support that warning. “It’s a fact, not hyperbole,” he said. In the accompanying post, Newsom urged voters to send Pappas to the Senate and help Goodlander reclaim a Democratic House majority. ... ## Former Trump Treasury official warns Fed rate hike would be a ‘mistake’ Former Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender warned Sunday that another interest rate hike could squeeze the economy without fixing the oil supply pressures he blamed for rising prices. “I do think they’re ultimately gonna raise rates, but I think it’s a mistake,” Faulkender said on “Sunday Morning Futures,” ahead of the Federal Reserve’s Oct. 28 decision. “They have no control over oil supply.” Faulkender argued higher borrowing costs would depress other parts of the economy while doing little to curb fuel demand from truckers or slow the construction of artificial intelligence data centers. He said easing tensions in the Middle East and productivity gains from AI could help cool inflation, warning a rate hike could hit after those benefits begin taking hold. Faulkender instead urged the Fed to focus on shrinking its balance sheet, arguing that would better anchor inflation expectations than a quarter-point rate increase. He also took aim at government expansion and tax increases, arguing they would shift resources away from businesses. ... ## Whatley vows to beat Cooper in North Carolina Senate showdown, pushes back on ad spending questions Republican Michael Whatley predicted victory in North Carolina’s Senate showdown Sunday, dismissing a Democratic edge and pushing back on questions about his campaign’s ad spending. “Well, we’re going to win this race,” Whatley told “The Sunday Briefing” when asked about Fox News Power Rankings rating the race “likely Democrat.” The former RNC chairman faces former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper for retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis’ seat. Asked about a Politico report that his campaign had no future traditional TV ad reservations booked, Whatley said spending had shifted toward digital and streaming. ... ## Ilhan Omar should be jailed, deported if citizenship fraud proven, Top House Republican says EXCLUSIVE: The highest-ranking House lawmaker from Rep. Ilhan Omar's home state is calling for the embattled progressive to be jailed and deported if it is found that she or her father lied on federal paperwork to get her U.S. citizenship. Omar, D-Minn., is under federal investigation over allegations she or her father lied about her birth year on immigration paperwork to obtain her citizenship when her family fled Somalia in the late 1990s. She and other Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., have denounced the probe as political persecution of one of President Donald Trump's detractors weeks before a critical election. ... ## Bernie Sanders admits Democrats failed working-class voters on economics, driving them to Trump Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., acknowledged on Saturday that Democrats failed working-class Americans economically, contributing to voters abandoning the party for President Donald Trump. ... arguing that its failure to address their financial ... ## Who will control the Senate after the midterm elections? Nine key races could decide Democrats have expanded their once-narrow path to reclaiming the Senate majority with just over two weeks until Election Day, but they'll need to win several competitive races to take control of the chamber. If Democrats ride a massive blue wave in the midterm elections, they could end up with 52 or even 53 seats in the next Senate. But if Republicans out-perform the polls, they could hold their majority, which currently stands at 53-47. Here's a look at the current battlefield and both parties' routes to securing a Senate majority in the midterms. The latest Power Rankings point to Democrats and Republicans each taking 47 seats in the midterms, leaving six races rated as true toss-ups. Additionally, three races are rated as leaners — one step shy of a toss-up. These nine showdowns will likely determine whether the Democrats make a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate or if the GOP holds the majority. "Nine races will determine control of the Senate, and on the polling alone, you could call any of them toss-ups," said Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings. The GOP is fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. Republicans also face a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and President Donald Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings. ... (AP Photo/Lisa Mascaro) House Speaker Mike Johnson believes Republicans will retain their narrow majority after the Nov. 3 elections, even as Democrats seek to capitalize on voter frustration and growing concerns about the GOP’s control of Congress. Johnson said he sees large crowds and strong candidates on the campaign trail, comparing the current political mood to the 2024 election that gave Republicans control of Washington. “It’s not going to be a giant majority,” Johnson said. “But I genuinely believe that we will have a working majority.” Johnson is campaigning across the country to defend Republican seats, while House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is preparing a first-100-days agenda if Democrats take back the chamber. items.title: Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's ...
items.excerpt: Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's what to know : NPR # Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's what to know October 18, 2026 2:38 PM ET Kristin Wright Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a media conference at the EU summit in Brussels, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP hide caption Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. officials remain at odds over disruptions to a key satellite communications service used by the Ukrainian military. Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday he believes the U.S. government is behind his military's loss of normal access to the Starshield and Starlink services, claiming tech firm SpaceX imposed the restrictions in response to a "message from [the] American government." Warning that the U.S. siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake," the Ukrainian leader claimed that the Starshield system has not been fully restored, despite what U.S. government officials have said publicly. In a post on X over the weekend, Zelenskyy said the restrictions on the system have hindered Ukraine's ability to intercept weapons launched by Russia, calling the consequences "very painful and unpleasant." The dispute comes after days of back and forth between Ukraine and the United States over the Starshield system. ### What are Starlink and Starshield? Starlink is a satellite internet network operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX to provide internet service to the U.S. and other counties. Since 2024, the U.S. Defense Department has shared a high-powered military version of the network called Starshield with Ukraine, which has cost the Pentagon billions of dollars. Ukraine relies on the network in its defenses against Russia's nearly five-year full-scale war. "We use Starlink to intercept the jet fighters that are hitting our civilians and killing families," said Zelenskyy online. "We also use Starlink for middle strikes on enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories. We were unable to do this when there were restrictions. And the third, most important thing is people. Our soldiers, who have been on the front line for weeks and months, are being delivered food and water using appropriate drones with Starlink." A policeman helps an elderly woman to walk out from a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Kateryna Klochko/AP hide caption ### Starshield controversy Zelenskyy said the disruptions to Starshield came without warning last week. He told NPR in an interview that losing normal access to the critical defense network had left his military's frontlines vulnerable. On X over the weekend, he said the network's speed hasn't been fully restored. It's unclear why Ukraine has experienced restricted access to Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that the U.S. government is responsible for the system, and that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." A bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Defense Department's inspector general to investigate how the system was disrupted. ### State Department reaction Speaking to reporters on Friday, President Trump denied interfering with Starshield. "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon. And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rejected Zelenskyy's claims that the disruptions to the system were deliberate. "It's just categorically false. No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn't use it," Rubio told reporters on Saturday, adding that Ukraine requested access to the system to carry out strikes deep inside Russia. "That's under conversation. It's under discussion right now of how they would want to use it," he said. Smoke billows into the sky following Ukrainian drone strikes on an industrial zone in St. Petersburg, Russia, on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. AP/AP hide caption ### America's faltering support for Ukraine The Starshield disruptions have renewed questions over the United States' commitment to supporting Ukraine against Russia's war, with tensions between President Trump and Zelenskyy growing over the past few days. Earlier this month, Trump moved to ease U.S. sanctions against Russia that had been passed by Congress. After Zelenskyy pushed back on the move, calling it a "weak decision by strong partners," Trump lashed out, criticizing Ukraine for striking Russian refineries, which he said was affecting U.S. diesel prices. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump said. The war of words has continued in the past few days, with the Ukrainian president outlining further areas of disagreement. On Sunday's Meet the Press, Zelenskyy also said that U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine concerning Russia ballistic missile attacks was blocked for three days, but has resumed. Ret. Navy Adm. Mark Montgomery told Here & Now's Scott Tong he believes the Starshield disruptions are a response by the White House to Zelenskyy's efforts to strike Russian oil refineries. "This is really a signal. It's a signal to stop attacking oil refineries and President Zelenskyy has properly pushed back on that," Montgomery said. He added it's an extremely vulnerable moment for Ukraine, as more Russian drones are able to get through. ### The war continues Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russia has launched more than 4,000 strike drones, bombs and missiles against his country over the past week. Russian attacks on Saturday night targeted energy substations leaving tens of thousands of people without electricity, according to Zelenskyy. Ukraine has responded to Moscow's strikes with its own attacks on Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian forces hit a major refinery southeast of Moscow last Thursday after Zelenskyy had said he was "done" following Trump's calls for an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine. On Sunday, Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot on fire in the Russian city of St. Petersburg, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia. items.excerpt: Harry Styles has enlisted filmmaker John Wilson to make a documentary about the singer’s current Madison Square Garden residency. In recent days, photos of Wilson — the offbeat documentarian behind his own How To With John Wilson HBO series and The History of Concrete — trailing Styles with camera in hand emerged on social media, leading fans to wonder if the two were collaborating on some sort of project. ... Variety has confirmed that the project in question is a documentary about Styles’ Together, Together 30-show residency at MSG, which started in August — when Wilson began filming — and runs through October 31. Not a traditional documentarian, Wilson’s Styles film will feature “a hybrid of live performances and a glimpse into Styles’ world,” Variety reported, adding that Wilson will dig deep into the residency with “authentic human stories of everyone involved in the tour —from the singer and his fans to countless others behind the scenes.” Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures and Styles are producing the documentary, with a theatrical release potentially in the works.
